## At a glance

**Guiding question:** Who bears the harm of a wrong decision, and who can object?\
**For:** clinicians, nurses, researchers and reviewers who have to justify how an alert is used; the core reading
needs no programming. · **Prerequisites:** the fracture alert and its predictive values in @sec-b09; absolute
frequencies and thresholds from @sec-b06.\
**In the course:** [W2 · Language models and
evidence](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w2-language-models-and-evidence.html)
(conversation card), [W3 · Diagnostics, prediction and external
evidence](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w3-diagnostics-prediction-evidence.html)
(errors by group), [W8 · Colloquium and
decision](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w8-colloquium-and-decision.html) ·
**Data:** synthetic (generated in the chapter) · **Core reading time:** about 10 minutes
:::

## Case and decision {#sec-b21-case}

It is 23:10 in the fictitious emergency department of @sec-b09, setting A. An 84-year-old patient who lives alone has
fallen onto her outstretched hand. The junior doctor sees no fracture on the wrist radiograph, but the image-analysis
tool shows "possible fracture – second look recommended". The radiology report will not be available before 08:30.
Three people look at the same alert. The patient wants to know whether she can sleep in her own bed. The nurse in
charge counts free trolleys and waiting alerts. A researcher who evaluates the tool asks
whether alerts in patients over 80 are wrong more often than in younger patients. The doctor has to act now: keep the
patient overnight, send her home with a splint and a morning call-back, or send her home without either. The patient
carries most of the consequence, so she must understand the options and be able to say no.

## Core reading {#sec-b21-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · recommended reading for W8, used in W2 and W3 · about 10 minutes · ends before ‘Decision exercise’
:::

```{r}
#| label: b21-core-numbers
#| echo: false
# Synthetic split of the 1,000 patients of setting A (B09) into four groups.
# The group counts are chosen so that the totals match B09 exactly: 50 fractures, 45 alerts among them,
# 950 without fracture, 95 alerts among them.
groups <- data.frame(
  group       = c("18–64 years", "65–79 years", "80 years and over", "Cast or metal implant"),
  examined    = c(560L, 280L, 120L, 40L),
  fracture    = c(22L, 14L, 12L, 2L),
  true_pos    = c(20L, 13L, 11L, 1L),
  false_pos   = c(38L, 27L, 26L, 4L)
)
groups$no_fracture <- groups$examined - groups$fracture
groups$false_neg   <- groups$fracture - groups$true_pos

# Wilson score interval for a proportion x/n (95%)
wilson <- function(x, n, level = 0.95) {
  z <- qnorm(1 - (1 - level) / 2)
  p <- x / n
  centre <- (p + z^2 / (2 * n)) / (1 + z^2 / n)
  half <- z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z^2 / (4 * n^2)) / (1 + z^2 / n)
  cbind(lower = centre - half, upper = centre + half)
}

fa  <- wilson(groups$false_pos, groups$no_fracture)   # false-alarm rate among patients without fracture
mis <- wilson(groups$false_neg, groups$fracture)      # miss rate among patients with fracture
sens_ci <- wilson(groups$true_pos, groups$fracture)   # sensitivity among patients with fracture
fa_rate  <- groups$false_pos / groups$no_fracture
sens     <- groups$true_pos / groups$fracture
old      <- 3                                         # row of the oldest group
young    <- 1
cast     <- 4
share_fp_old  <- groups$false_pos[old] / sum(groups$false_pos)
share_pat_old <- groups$examined[old] / sum(groups$examined)
fmt_ci <- function(ci) sprintf("%s to %s", cdsr_percent(ci[1]), cdsr_percent(ci[2]))
stopifnot(sum(groups$examined) == 1000, sum(groups$fracture) == 50,
          sum(groups$true_pos) == 45, sum(groups$false_pos) == 95)
```

**From a predictive value to a distribution of harm.** In setting A of @sec-b09, 5% of the patients examined have a
fracture, and the tool's sensitivity and specificity are both 90% (*assumptions*). Of 1,000 patients, 140 receive an
alert; 95 of them have no fracture, and 5 patients with a fracture receive no alert. Ethics begins where these counts
meet people. A false alarm can mean an unnecessary splint, an extra radiograph, a night on a trolley or a delayed
discharge. A missed fracture can mean a scaphoid that is not immobilised, weeks of pain and, later, an operation. The
two errors do not fall on the same people, and they do not weigh the same for everyone. For a 30-year-old, a night in
the department is an inconvenience. For an 84-year-old living alone, it brings a risk of delirium and falls. The
question is therefore not only "how often is the tool wrong?" but "who carries each kind of error, and could they have
chosen differently?"

**Several lenses, one alert.** Clinical ethics usually asks four questions: is the person's autonomy respected, does
the action benefit them, does it avoid harm, and are benefits and burdens shared fairly? The WHO guidance on AI for
health adds that humans should remain in control of medical decisions and that people should understand the role an
AI system plays in their care [@who2024lmm, Box 1, p. 5]. It also names automation bias, in which a clinician overlooks
an error that a human should have spotted, and the gradual loss of skills that makes it harder to overrule an algorithm
[@who2024lmm, pp. 11–12]. A further lens is professional responsibility: the doctor remains accountable for the
decision, whatever the box says. @tbl-b21-perspectives applies these lenses to the three people in the case.

| | Patient, 84, lives alone | Nurse in charge | Researcher evaluating the tool |
|---|---|---|---|
| What matters most | Sleeping at home; not being sent away with a fracture | Safe care for everyone in the department tonight | A valid estimate of how the tool behaves in this population |
| Harm they see | Night on a trolley, delirium, a fall; or a missed fracture | Alerts that bind staff and trolleys; alert fatigue | Errors concentrated in a group that the overall figures hide |
| What they need | Plain numbers, real options, a contact person | A named person who reviews alerts, within planned time | Prespecified subgroups, counts with denominators, intervals |
| What they can object to | Staying overnight; any of the options offered | Being made responsible for reviews without time | A deployment plan that ignores an unexplained subgroup signal |

: Three perspectives on the same alert. Fictional roles; the table is a structure for discussion, not a survey result. {#tbl-b21-perspectives}

**Errors by group need denominators.** @fig-b21-subgroups splits the 1,000 patients of setting A into four groups.
**The key assumption: the group counts are *synthetic* and were chosen so that the totals match setting A exactly;
they show what a local evaluation would have to measure, not what any real tool does.** Patients aged 80 and over
make up `r cdsr_percent(share_pat_old, 0)` of those examined but receive `r groups$false_pos[old]` of the
`r sum(groups$false_pos)` false alarms (`r cdsr_percent(share_fp_old)`). Their false-alarm rate is
`r cdsr_percent(fa_rate[old])` (`r groups$false_pos[old]`/`r groups$no_fracture[old]`; 95% interval
`r fmt_ci(fa[old, ])`), compared with `r cdsr_percent(fa_rate[young])` (`r groups$false_pos[young]`/`r groups$no_fracture[young]`;
`r fmt_ci(fa[young, ])`) in patients aged 18–64. Patients with a plaster cast or metal implant are a different case.
Only `r groups$fracture[cast]` of them have a fracture, and the tool flags `r groups$true_pos[cast]`. A sensitivity of
`r cdsr_percent(sens[cast], 0)` with an interval from `r fmt_ci(sens_ci[cast, ])` means: we
do not know. The intervals are Wilson score intervals, which behave well with small counts
[@wilson1927interval; @brown2001interval]; the general idea is explained in
[Methods in R: Confidence intervals](https://r-heller.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-01-foundations.html#sec-chapters-01-foundations-confidence-intervals-introduction).

```{r}
#| label: fig-b21-subgroups
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Error rates of the fracture alert by patient group in setting A, with 95% Wilson intervals. Left: false alarms among patients without fracture; right: missed fractures among patients with fracture. Labels give numerator/denominator. Synthetic counts that add up to the 1,000 patients of setting A in B09; independent unit: patient (n = 1,000; denominators per panel and group as labelled)."
#| fig-alt: "Two side-by-side panels with four patient groups on the vertical axis: 18 to 64 years, 65 to 79 years, 80 years and over, and cast or metal implant. Each group has a point with a horizontal interval. Left panel, false alarms among patients without fracture: 38 of 538 (7.1%), 27 of 266 (10.2%), 26 of 108 (24.1%, interval roughly 17 to 33%), and 4 of 38 (10.5%). Right panel, missed fractures among patients with fracture: 2 of 22, 1 of 14, 1 of 12, and 1 of 2, where the last interval spans most of the scale. The figure shows a higher false-alarm rate in the oldest group and great uncertainty in the small cast group."
library(ggplot2)
plot_df <- rbind(
  data.frame(panel = "False alarms among patients without fracture",
             group = groups$group, x = groups$false_pos, n = groups$no_fracture,
             rate = fa_rate, lower = fa[, "lower"], upper = fa[, "upper"]),
  data.frame(panel = "Missed fractures among patients with fracture",
             group = groups$group, x = groups$false_neg, n = groups$fracture,
             rate = groups$false_neg / groups$fracture, lower = mis[, "lower"], upper = mis[, "upper"])
)
plot_df$group <- factor(plot_df$group, levels = rev(groups$group))
plot_df$label <- sprintf("%d/%d", plot_df$x, plot_df$n)
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = rate, y = group, shape = group, colour = group)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), width = 0.25, linewidth = 0.7, orientation = "y") +
  geom_point(size = 2.8) +
  geom_text(aes(x = upper, label = label), hjust = -0.2, size = 3.3, colour = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 2, labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 30)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(v) cdsr_percent(v, 0), limits = c(0, 1.12),
                     breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = rev(cdsr_shapes), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = rev(unname(cdsr_colours[c("blue", "orange", "red", "grey")])), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Error rate (95% Wilson interval)", y = NULL,
       caption = "Synthetic data · setting A of B09 · n = 1,000 patients; denominators as labelled") +
  theme_cdsr()
```

A group finding like this is a reason to look closer, not yet a proven property of the tool. Published examples show
why the look is necessary. Chest radiograph classifiers underdiagnosed under-served patient groups, most clearly in
intersectional subgroups such as Hispanic female patients [@seyyedkalantari2021underdiagnosis; *published*]. A widely
used population-health algorithm predicted health-care costs rather than illness, so that Black patients with the same
score were sicker than White patients [@obermeyer2019bias; *published*]. In both cases a good overall figure hid a
systematic burden on one group.

**"Human in the loop" is a job description.** The phrase protects patients only if it names someone. Four conditions
make it real. First, a named role on the rota, not "the team". Second, time: in setting A the tool creates about 1.6
alerts per shift (@sec-b09), and their review must be part of the planned workload. Third, competence: the reviewer
knows the tool's typical failure modes, including the groups in @fig-b21-subgroups. Fourth, a real possibility to
override: disregarding the alert must be as easy as following it and must not require a written justification each
time. For high-risk AI systems the [EU AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng) requires deployers to assign human oversight to people with the
necessary competence, training and authority, and to support them (Art. 26(2)); the system must let them stay aware
of automation bias and disregard or override its output (Art. 14(4)(b) and (d)) [@eu2024aiact]. For AI that is part of
a medical device needing a notified body, these duties apply from 2 August 2028 (@sec-b22). Ethically, the four
conditions apply from the first night. A systematic review found workload, task complexity and time pressure among the factors that increase
automation bias [@goddard2012automation].

**A real choice, checked with teach-back.** Shared decision making moves from introducing the choice to describing
options to helping the person decide [@elwyn2012sdm]. A choice is only real if the organisation has created the
options: the splint is in stock, the morning call-back has a named slot, and someone can take the patient home at
midnight. Teach-back closes the loop: the clinician asks the patient to explain in her own words what the alert means
and what she will do. It tests the explanation, not the patient. In an observational study of patients with diabetes
and limited health literacy, physicians checked understanding in only 12 of 61 visits; where they did, glycaemic
control was better, with very wide confidence intervals [@schillinger2003teachback; *published*].

**Question for the workshop:** The night team can offer only two of the three options from the case. Which option
would you keep at all costs, and which group of patients would lose most if it disappeared?

## Decision exercise {#sec-b21-exercise}

The exercise has two parts: a short R calculation that makes the group errors checkable, and a conversation in which
the result has to be explained to the patient.

**Part 1 – recompute the group errors.** The table below is the input of @fig-b21-subgroups. The Wilson interval is
written out as a small function and checked against `prop.test()`, whose interval without continuity correction is
the same score interval.

```{r}
#| label: b21-lab-wilson
# Synthetic counts for setting A (n = 1,000 patients)
groups[, c("group", "examined", "fracture", "true_pos", "false_pos")]

# Check 1: the groups reproduce the totals of B09 (45/140 alerts with fracture)
stopifnot(sum(groups$true_pos) / (sum(groups$true_pos) + sum(groups$false_pos)) == 45 / 140)

# Check 2: own Wilson function equals prop.test() without continuity correction
for (i in seq_len(nrow(groups))) {
  # prop.test() warns about its chi-squared p-value for small counts; the interval itself is unaffected
  ref <- suppressWarnings(prop.test(groups$false_pos[i], groups$no_fracture[i], correct = FALSE))$conf.int
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(fa[i, ]), as.numeric(ref), tolerance = 1e-10)))
}

# Result table: rates with intervals, per group
result <- data.frame(
  group            = groups$group,
  false_alarms     = sprintf("%d/%d", groups$false_pos, groups$no_fracture),
  false_alarm_rate = cdsr_percent(fa_rate),
  fa_95_interval   = apply(fa, 1, fmt_ci),
  ppv              = cdsr_percent(groups$true_pos / (groups$true_pos + groups$false_pos)),
  share_of_false_alarms = cdsr_percent(groups$false_pos / sum(groups$false_pos))
)
result

# Check 3: the intervals of the oldest and the youngest group do not overlap (in this synthetic example)
stopifnot(fa[old, "lower"] > fa[young, "upper"])
# Check 4: the cast group's sensitivity interval is wider than 0.75 - too few fractures to say anything
stopifnot(diff(sens_ci[cast, ]) > 0.75)
```

The calculation shows two different findings. In the oldest group the false-alarm rate is higher, and the interval
excludes the rate of the youngest group. In the cast group nothing can be concluded about sensitivity, because two
fractures are not a denominator. Both findings change the conversation with the patient: her group has a lower
predictive value (`r result$ppv[old]`) than the department as a whole (32.1%).

**Part 2 – the conversation.** Work in threes: doctor, patient, observer. The doctor has five minutes. The script
below is a starting point, not a text to read aloud.

::: {.callout-note title="Conversation card: alert, options, teach-back"}
1. **Name the situation.** "The computer program that looks at X-rays has marked your wrist. That does not mean it is
   broken. It means a specialist should look again."
2. **Give the number in people.** "In patients of your age in our department, about 3 in 10 of these marks turn out
   to be a real fracture." (In a real department this figure must come from local data; here it is the synthetic
   `r result$ppv[old]`.)
3. **Offer the real options.** "You can stay here tonight and we will have the answer in the morning. Or you can go
   home with a removable splint; we will phone you before 10:00 with the result and tell you whether to come back. If
   the pain or swelling gets worse, you come back at once."
4. **Ask what matters.** "What is most important to you tonight?"
5. **Teach-back.** "I want to make sure I explained this well. Could you tell me in your own words what the mark
   means and what you will do if the pain gets worse?"
6. **Document** the choice, the reason the patient gave and who will make the call-back.
:::

The observer notes whether the doctor gave the number in people, whether both options were presented with their
downsides, whether the patient's answer in step 5 was correct and whether the doctor corrected the explanation, not the
patient.

**Expected result.** A documented decision that the patient can repeat in her own words, a call-back owner with a
time, and a note of the predictive value used for her group, marked as local or synthetic.\
**Alternative.** The doctor calls the on-call senior to review the image now. This avoids the night-time uncertainty
but uses scarce senior time; it is the right choice if the department has planned it as part of the reviewer's
role.\
**Residual question.** Who decides whether the call-back option is offered at all, and what happens to patients who
cannot be reached by phone?

## Counter-check {#sec-b21-countercheck}

Change the target population before you calculate. Suppose the same group-specific error rates apply in setting B
of @sec-b09, where 20% of patients have a fracture. *Predict first:* does the predictive value in the oldest group rise
or fall, and does the oldest group's share of false alarms change?

```{r}
#| label: b21-countercheck
# Setting B: same group sizes, more fractures (synthetic, 200 in total)
fracture_b <- c(90, 60, 40, 10)
stopifnot(sum(fracture_b) == 200)
tp_b <- fracture_b * sens                                     # expected true alerts
fp_b <- (groups$examined - fracture_b) * fa_rate              # expected false alerts
data.frame(group = groups$group,
           ppv_setting_A = cdsr_percent(groups$true_pos / (groups$true_pos + groups$false_pos)),
           ppv_setting_B = cdsr_percent(tp_b / (tp_b + fp_b)),
           share_false_alarms_B = cdsr_percent(fp_b / sum(fp_b)))

# Check: PPV in the oldest group rises with prevalence
stopifnot(tp_b[old] / (tp_b[old] + fp_b[old]) > groups$true_pos[old] / (groups$true_pos[old] + groups$false_pos[old]))

# Second counter-check: ten times as many patients with cast, same rates
mis_big <- wilson(10 * groups$false_neg[cast], 10 * groups$fracture[cast])
c(width_n2 = diff(mis[cast, ]), width_n20 = diff(mis_big[1, ]))
stopifnot(diff(mis_big[1, ]) < diff(mis[cast, ]))
```

In setting B the predictive value rises in every group, because a larger share of patients has a fracture. The oldest
group still carries a disproportionate share of the false alarms. Prevalence changes the predictive value, not the
group's error rate. The second check shows that a larger denominator narrows the interval but leaves the point
estimate unchanged; it would take many more patients with casts before the miss rate could be called high or low. A
practical consequence: the overall specificity of 90% in @sec-b09 is itself an average over a case mix. If the case
mix shifts towards older patients, the department's overall false-alarm rate rises even if the tool does not change.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b21-consequences}

**An ethically questionable recommendation changes the plan.** Suppose the supplier proposes to sort the radiology
worklist by alert status: flagged images are reported first, unflagged images up to 24 hours later. On average this
looks efficient. In setting A, however, 5 of the 50 fractures are unflagged and would wait longest, and in the cast
group the tool missed one of two fractures – nobody knows how often it misses more. The burden of delay would fall on a group for which the tool is least
reliable and whose patients cannot know that their image was put at the back of the queue. @tbl-b21-plan shows how
the deployment plan changes.

| Element | Plan before the review | Plan after the review |
|---|---|---|
| Worklist order | Sorted by alert status | Clinical order unchanged; the alert only adds a second-look flag |
| Human oversight | "Clinician in the loop" | Named on-call senior per shift; review time planned per alert; override without justification form |
| Cast or metal implant | Included | Excluded from the alert until a local evaluation with enough fractures exists; always senior review |
| Patients 80 and over | No special rule | Group-specific predictive value reported monthly with interval; call-back option guaranteed |
| Conversation | Information leaflet | Conversation card with teach-back; documented choice and call-back owner |

: Deployment plan for the fracture alert before and after the ethical review. Fictional plan; the elements are examples. {#tbl-b21-plan}

**Regulation and data protection.** Excluding a patient group or changing what the alert is used for may change the
intended purpose of the product; @sec-b22 shows why this needs a dated note before go-live. Group analyses require
processing age and possibly further characteristics. Ethnicity or disability would be special categories of personal
data under the GDPR; the amended AI Act now sets strict conditions under which providers of high-risk systems may
exceptionally process such data to detect and correct bias (Art. 4a, inserted by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force
since 27 July 2026) [@eu2026omnibus]. @sec-b23 covers the data-protection side.

**Security and availability.** If the tool fails, the plan must still give every patient a timely report. This
fallback is the regular reporting pathway, tested as described in @sec-b24.

::: {.callout-note title="The incident from the ethics perspective"}
In the fictional incident of Part VI, an excerpt from a radiology report appears in a service provider's support log,
and the installed model version differs from the approved one. From an ethics perspective the first questions are:
which patients are affected, who among them is particularly burdened (for example by a sensitive diagnosis in the
excerpt), and who explains the situation to them in plain language? A good answer names a reachable contact person,
offers to answer questions by phone and in writing, and does not wait for the end of the technical analysis to decide
whether patients deserve an explanation. Whether a formal notification is legally required is a separate question
(@sec-b23).
:::

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b21-lookup}

**Reviewer question.** Were the subgroups prespecified, and does the report give numerator, denominator and an
interval for each error rate in each subgroup? A sentence such as "performance was similar across age groups" without
counts cannot be checked
([Methods in R: Subgroup analyses](https://r-heller.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-14-clinical.html#sec-chapters-14-clinical-subgroup-analysis)).

**Self-test.** A paediatric emergency department wants to use the same tool for children aged 6–15. Growth plates
can look like fracture lines. A local check finds 18 false alarms among 60 children without fracture and 3 missed
fractures among 15 children with fracture. The supplier says: "Overall accuracy in children is 72%." What would you
report to the department, and which ethical question would you raise before go-live?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Report the two errors separately with their denominators and intervals: false alarms 18/60 = 30.0% (Wilson 95%
interval about 19.9% to 42.5%) and missed fractures 3/15 = 20.0% (about 7.0% to 45.2%). Overall accuracy mixes the
two and hides that each child without fracture has roughly a one-in-three chance of a false alarm. The ethical
question is who bears the burden: false alarms in children mean extra radiation and immobilisation; misses mean
untreated fractures in growing bones. Before go-live, the department needs a named reviewer for paediatric alerts, an
explanation for parents and a decision on whether the evidence (15 fractures) is enough at all. Children were not part
of the intended population in the setting A data; using the tool for them is a change of intended purpose
(@sec-b22).
:::

**Annotated sources.**

- @who2024lmm – the six WHO principles (Box 1) and the description of automation bias and skills loss; used here for
  autonomy and human control.
- @eu2024aiact – Art. 14(4) and Art. 26(2) translate human oversight into duties of providers and deployers; used for
  the four conditions of a real "human in the loop".
- @eu2026omnibus – inserts Art. 4a on processing special categories of data for bias detection; relevant to the design
  of subgroup analyses.
- @wilson1927interval and @brown2001interval – the original score interval and the comparison showing why simple
  intervals for proportions fail with small counts.
- @seyyedkalantari2021underdiagnosis and @obermeyer2019bias – published cases in which good overall performance hid
  systematic harm to specific groups.
- @goddard2012automation – systematic review of automation bias and its mediators, including workload and time
  pressure.
- @elwyn2012sdm and @schillinger2003teachback – a practical model of shared decision making and an observational study
  of checking patients' understanding.

## Further reading {#sec-b21-further}

- @sec-b09 – the alert, the two settings and the predictive values on which this chapter builds.
- @sec-b06 – thresholds and absolute frequencies, to weigh false alarms against missed fractures.
- @sec-b20 – how group-specific error rates enter a monitoring plan with escalation and stop criteria.
- @sec-b22 and @sec-b23 – when a change in the patient group changes the intended purpose, and how group data may be
  processed.
- [Scientometrics in R: Ethics and responsible metrics](https://r-heller.github.io/scientometrics-in-r/ethics-and-responsible-metrics.html)
  – why a single indicator should not decide about people; transferable to alert metrics.
- [Scientometrics in R: Gender and equity analysis](https://r-heller.github.io/scientometrics-in-r/gender-and-equity-analysis.html#gender-pitfalls)
  – pitfalls when comparing groups, including small groups and inferred attributes.
- [CTTIR Courses: TRIPOD-AI, fairness auditing, reproducibility at scale](https://cttir.github.io/courses/course4_ml_highdim/labs/lab_week4_session5.html)
  – a lab that audits model errors by group.
- [Strategy in R: Fairness in machine learning](https://r-heller.github.io/strategy-in-r/sec-fairness-ml.html) – formal
  fairness criteria and why they cannot all hold at once.
